slides.0.title: Course Introduction
slides.0.content:
The greatness of Bordeaux wine lies not only in its exceptional terroir, but in the masterful art of blending practised by its winemakers. Blending (Assemblage) is the most central skill in Bordeaux — the craft of fusing wines from different varieties and different plots into a perfect whole.

A top-tier Bordeaux red is typically blended from 3–5 varieties: Cabernet Sauvignon provides structure and aging potential, Merlot contributes suppleness and fruit, and Cabernet Franc adds elegance and complexity. Fine-tuning blend ratios can create dramatically different styles — this is where the winemaker's art and science meet in perfect harmony.

Learning Objectives

🧪 Master the classic Bordeaux blending ratios and principles

Understand the stylistic differences between Left Bank Cabernet-dominant (60–80%) and Right Bank Merlot-dominant (60–90%) blends, and learn variety role allocation

🍇 Understand the unique role of each grape variety

Gain an in-depth understanding of how the five main varieties (CS, Merlot, CF, Petit Verdot, Malbec) function and contribute in a blend

🎨 Explore the blending philosophy of top winemakers

Learn how the winemakers of Château Margaux, Haut-Brion and other great estates make decisions between tradition and innovation

📊 Analyse vintage variation and its blending strategy implications

Understand how blending strategy should adapt when facing warm versus cool vintages, and the impact of climate change

🔬 Grasp the application of modern technology in blending

From spectral analysis to AI-assisted blending systems, understand how technology enhances traditional blending artistry
slides.1.title: Fundamentals of Blending
slides.1.subtitle: From Single Variety to Perfect Harmony
slides.2.title: Why Blend?
slides.2.content:
Three Core Motivations Behind Bordeaux Blending
🎵 Creating Complexity
A single variety can express pure varietal character, but blending creates a complexity and balance that no single variety can achieve alone. Like the harmonious interplay of different instruments in a symphony, each variety plays a unique role.
✨ 1 + 1 > 2 — the whole exceeds the sum of its parts
🌧️ Spreading Risk
Different varieties have different sensitivities to weather at each growth stage. Cabernet Sauvignon ripens later and is more susceptible to autumn rain; Merlot buds earlier but is more heat-resistant. Blending provides natural risk diversification against vintage variation.
🌿 In challenging vintages, variety diversification is insurance
📊 Ensuring Consistency
Great châteaux must maintain their signature style across different vintages. By adjusting blending ratios — more Merlot in cool years, more CS in hot years — winemakers preserve the château's fundamental character despite year-to-year variation.
🏆 Château style consistency is the foundation of brand value
💡 Bordeaux Blending Philosophy: Blending is not to conceal deficiencies, but to create a perfection that transcends any single variety. Each adjustment reflects both the winemaker's philosophy and their response to the vintage.
slides.3.title: The Three Pillars of Bordeaux Blending
slides.3.content:
👑 Cabernet Sauvignon
The King of Structure
Provides the skeleton and power — firm tannins, deep colour, blackcurrant aromas — conferring remarkable aging potential. The soul variety of Left Bank blends.
Typical Ratio
40–70%
Aging Potential
20–50 yrs
Blackcurrant · Cedar · Lead pencil · Structured tannins
🍇 Merlot
The Harmoniser
Brings roundness and approachability — plum, chocolate and early-drinking appeal — softening CS's hard edges. The dominant variety on the Right Bank.
Typical Ratio
10–60%
Aging Potential
5–20 yrs
Plum · Chocolate · Round tannins · Early accessibility
🌸 Cabernet Franc
The Elegance Enhancer
Adds elegance and floral notes — violet, pencil shavings, spice — lifting the blend's aromatic complexity and contributing fresh acidity to balance ripeness.
Typical Ratio
3–20%
Aging Potential
10–30 yrs
Violet · Pencil shavings · Fresh acidity · Spice
🌿 Petit Verdot
The Seasoning Spice
Used in very small proportions (1–5%), but its contribution is remarkable: deep inky colour, concentrated spice and violet aromas, with firm tannins that add structure and colour intensity. Requires a warm year to ripen fully.
Ink · Violet · Spice · Used only in good years
🍁 Malbec
The Texture Softener
Once widely planted in Bordeaux, now used in tiny amounts (0–3%). Contributes deep colour, plummy fruit and velvety texture. More famous today in Argentina, where it is the flagship variety.
Deep colour · Plum · Velvet texture · Rare in Bordeaux today

slides.7.title: Variety Roles Explained in Detail
slides.7.content:
🏛️ CS — The Architect
Like the steel frame of a building, Cabernet Sauvignon provides the solid structural foundation of the wine. Its high tannin content and deep colour confer powerful aging potential and the ability to develop complex tertiary aromas over decades.
Core contribution: Structure · Tannins · Aging potential · Blackcurrant flavours
🍇 Merlot — The Harmoniser
Merlot acts as a gentle harmoniser: its round texture and generous fruit soften Cabernet Sauvignon's hard edges while filling the mid-palate gaps, making the blend more accessible from an earlier stage.
Core contribution: Roundness · Fruit richness · Early accessibility · Plum flavours
🌸 Cabernet Franc — The Perfumer
Cabernet Franc is the blend's perfumer, adding floral and spicy top notes — violet, pencil shavings, red berry — while contributing lively acidity to prevent the blend from feeling heavy or flat.
Core contribution: Elegance · Floral aroma · Acidity · Spice
🌿 Petit Verdot — The Seasoning
Used sparingly (1–5%), Petit Verdot acts like a potent seasoning: adding ink-dark colour depth, concentrated violet aromas and firm tannins that enhance structure and longevity. Only used in warm years when it ripens fully.
Core contribution: Colour depth · Violet · Structure · Only in top vintages
🍁 Malbec — The Texture Softener
Rarely used in Bordeaux today (0–3%), Malbec contributes deep colour, plummy fruit and velvety texture. Once widespread in Bordeaux, it has largely migrated to Argentina where it now reigns as the flagship grape.
Core contribution: Colour depth · Plum texture · Now more prominent in Mendoza
💡 The Five-Variety Orchestra
Each variety has its irreplaceable role: CS lays the foundation, Merlot adds flesh, CF sprinkles perfume, PV sharpens the colour and adds depth, and Malbec provides a velvety finish. A masterful winemaker knows how to conduct them together — creating harmony that transcends any soloist.

slides.10.title: Decoding the Blending Ratios of the Five First Growths
slides.10.content:
👑 Château Lafite
Pauillac · Elegance School
Pursues the "perfect balance of elegance and power" — less CS than Latour, more Merlot to soften the structure. Creates silky tannins and mineral character; aging potential 30–50 years.
CS 70% + M 25% + CF 3% + PV 2%
🎨 Silky tannins · Cedarwood · Lead pencil mineral
💪 Château Latour
Pauillac · Power School
The highest CS ratio among the First Growths, pursues maximum structure and longevity — the most "muscular" and long-lived First Growth. Great vintages need 20+ years before opening.
CS 75–80% + M 15–20% + CF 4% + PV 1%
💪 Powerful tannins · Deep colour · Iron minerality
🌹 Château Margaux
Margaux · Floral School
Renowned for its floral aromatics and delicate texture, with the highest CF ratio among the Left Bank First Growths. Pure Cabernet Sauvignon is used for the grand vin only.
CS 75% + M 20% + CF 5%
🌹 Floral · Delicate · Feminine elegance
🌿 Château Haut-Brion
Pessac-Léognan · Terroir School
The most unique blending style among the First Growths — significantly higher Merlot ratio than Médoc peers, reflecting the clay-gravel terroir of Pessac-Léognan. Known for its smoky, tobacco and earthy complexity.
CS 45% + M 37% + CF 18%
🌿 Earthy · Tobacco · Smoky minerality
🏰 Château Mouton Rothschild
Pauillac · Bold School
The highest CS proportion among all First Growths, pursuing extreme concentration and depth. Famous for its expressive cassis, cedar and graphite aromas. Each year's label features an artwork by a world-renowned artist.
CS 80–85% + M 10% + CF 8% + PV 2%
🎨 Cassis · Graphite · Cedar concentration
💡 Key Insight: Five châteaux all in Pauillac or nearby, yet each pursues a radically different style — proof that blending ratios directly shape a château's identity and market positioning.
slides.11.title: The Evolution of Blending Ratios
slides.11.content:
📈 Historical Trend Analysis
Over the past 50 years, blending ratios across Bordeaux have changed significantly. Climate change has made Cabernet Sauvignon easier to ripen, while market demand for earlier accessibility has driven an increase in Merlot proportions.
1970s vs 2020s: Merlot ratios broadly up 5–15%
🔬 The Impact of Technology
Modern winemaking techniques such as optical sorting and micro-oxygenation allow winemakers to control each variety's expression far more precisely, opening up greater creative freedom in the blending process.
Precision winemaking: modern technology makes blending more scientific
🌍 Market-Driven Adjustments
Younger consumers prefer wines with richer fruit and softer tannins, prompting many estates to increase Merlot plantings or adopt gentler extraction methods to deliver earlier-drinking pleasure.
Consumer trend: shifting from age-required to early-accessible

slides.14.title: The Complete Blending Decision Timeline
slides.14.content:
⏱️ Phase One
1 month post-harvest · Initial Assessment
Evaluate the quality potential of each variety, analyse each plot's character, and establish the basic blending direction. At this stage, keep an open mind and avoid drawing conclusions prematurely.
🎯 Identify the lead variety and rough ratio framework (e.g. CS 65–75%)
🔬 Phase Two
3–6 months post-harvest · Precision Blending
Taste through 50–100 individual barrels, carry out 5–10 small-scale trial blends, and evaluate each combination for balance, complexity, and aging potential.
🎯 Confirm final blending ratios (precise to 1%)
✨ Phase Three
12–18 months post-harvest · Refinement
Evaluate the blend's integration and aging development before bottling; make minor adjustments (1–3%) based on tasting feedback. Confirm quality consistency between the grand vin and second wine.
🎯 Final confirmation for bottling; decide grand vin / second wine split

slides.15.title: Master Interview: Michel Rolland on the Art of Blending
slides.15.content:
International wine consultant · advises over 100 châteaux worldwide
Michel Rolland's blending philosophy — including Pétrus, Le Pin, Angelus and other top estates
Q1 · What is the most important principle?
"Balance is at the core of everything. But I don't mean a mathematical balance — I mean harmony on the palate. Every vintage, every plot has its own personality, and my job is to make them sing the most beautiful chord together. In a great blended wine, you should not be able to distinguish which is the Cabernet and which is the Merlot — what you should experience is a perfectly integrated whole."
🎵 Pursue palate harmony, not mathematical ratios
Q2 · How does vintage variation affect blending?
"In a warm year, I increase the proportion of Cabernet Franc to maintain freshness and acidity; in a cool year, I may add more Merlot to supply roundness and fruit. The key is to understand the character of each vintage and then use blending to optimise its expression. There is no fixed formula — every vintage is a new challenge and a new opportunity."
🌡️ Flexible strategy: adjust ratios according to the vintage's character
Q3 · Advice for young winemakers?
"First, learn to taste — develop a keen and discerning palate. Taste different wines every day and train yourself to detect subtle differences. Second, understand how each variety actually performs across different soils and vintages. Most importantly, have patience — blending is an art that takes time and accumulated experience."
📚 Palate training + varietal understanding + patience and experience

slides.21.title: Vintage Variation and Blending Strategy
slides.21.subtitle: Adapting to Nature, Creating Consistency
slides.22.title: How Vintage Characteristics Influence Blending
slides.22.content:
☀️ Warm Vintage Strategy
In warm years, grapes are highly ripe with abundant sugar, but may lack acidity. Winemakers typically increase the Cabernet Franc proportion to lift freshness, or select fruit from cooler plots to balance the overall style.
2003 · 2005 · 2009 · 2010: Classic warm-year challenges
🌧️ Cool Vintage Wisdom
In cool years, grapes have high acidity but may lack full ripeness. Winemakers raise the Merlot proportion to add fruit and roundness, while selecting fruit from the warmest plots as the blend's foundation.
2007 · 2008 · 2013 · 2014: Years that tested blending skill
⚖️ Ideal Vintage Balance
In climatically ideal vintages, all varieties can reach perfect ripeness. The winemaker's task here is restraint — not to over-intervene, but to let each variety express its finest character and create a harmonious whole.
2000 · 2016 · 2019 · 2020: Near-perfect balanced vintages
slides.23.title: Case Study: 2010 vs. 2013 Vintage Blending Strategies
slides.23.content:
☀️ 2010 — Hot & Dry · Near-Perfect Year
Challenge: Over-ripeness · Low acidity · High alcohol · Powerful tannins
Strategy: ↑ CF (+5–10%) for freshness · Select cooler plots · Shorter maceration
Pichon Baron Case:
Standard: CS 70% + Merlot 25% + CF 5%
2010: CS 65% + Merlot 23% + CF 12%
→ CF doubled ↑, scored RP 98
🌧️ 2013 — Cool & Rainy · Challenging Year
Challenge: Under-ripeness · Excessive acidity · Thin fruit · Green tannins
Strategy: ↑ Merlot (+10–15%) for roundness · Strict fruit selection · Extended maceration
Lynch-Bages Case:
Standard: CS 73% + Merlot 15% + CF 10% + PV 2%
2013: CS 60% + Merlot 30% + CF 8% + PV 2%
→ Merlot doubled ↑, scored RP 90

slides.24.title: Modern Technology and Blending Innovation
slides.24.subtitle: Technology Empowering Traditional Artistry
slides.25.title: Modern Blending Technology Innovations
slides.25.content:
🔬 Precision Analytical Technology
Modern laboratories can analyse the chemical composition of each component with great precision — hundreds of compounds including phenolics, pigments, and aromatic molecules. Data shifts blending decisions from pure intuition to data-supported instinct, improving accuracy by 30%.
Chemical analysis + sensory evaluation = more precise blending decisions
💨 The Micro-Oxygenation Revolution
Precisely controlling oxygen exposure (0.5–2 mg/L/month) and timing softens tannins, stabilises pigments, and promotes the polymerisation of aromatic molecules — helping diverse components integrate into a harmonious whole and shortening the blending-to-bottling cycle.
Micro-oxygenation accelerates harmonious integration by 6–12 months
💻 Digital Management Systems
Advanced estates use specialist software to record every detail of each blend: variety, plot, fermentation parameters, sensory scores, and final ratios. After years of data accumulation, the system can identify historical patterns and provide a scientific reference for future decisions.
Big data: 10 years of blending history becomes a decision-support system
slides.26.title: Innovative Blending Tools Used by Top Châteaux
slides.26.content:
🔍 Spectral Analyser
Near-infrared spectroscopy (NIR) technology analyses the chemical composition of wine within minutes — instantly measuring total phenolics, tannins, and anthocyanins, predicting aging potential, and ensuring batch-to-batch quality consistency.
Analysis time: reduced from 2–3 days to 5 minutes
🖥️ Blending Software Systems
AI-assisted blending ratio calculation and simulation instantly models the theoretical outcome of dozens of combinations, integrating historical data and predictive models. Some systems now incorporate machine learning, drawing on 1,000+ blending cases to provide intelligent recommendations.
65% of mid-to-large estates use software · €2K–10K/year
👃 Sensory Analysis Room
A professional tasting environment designed to ISO 8589 standards, eliminating interference from light, temperature, and ambient odour. Fitted with individual tasting booths, standardised glasses, and a recording system to ensure objective assessment during blending evaluation.
20±2°C · Humidity 60–70% · Neutral lighting

slides.28.title: New World vs. Old World Blending Philosophy
slides.28.subtitle: A Dialogue Between Tradition and Innovation
slides.29.title: The Three Global Schools of Blending Philosophy
slides.29.content:
🏛️ Bordeaux: Terroir Guardian
Strict adherence to traditional variety combinations (CS + Merlot + CF), emphasising pure terroir expression and pursuing elegant balance. Prized for exceptional long-aging potential (20–50 years) and deep respect for AOC regulations.
Terroir expression · Elegant balance · Ultra-long aging · Tradition
🌟 Napa Valley: Fruit Pioneer
Innovative variety combinations (incorporating Syrah, Malbec, etc.), emphasising concentrated fruit and immediate enjoyment. Prioritises early accessibility (3–10 years), with style driven by market preferences.
Rich fruit · Early accessibility · Innovative blends · Market-driven
🔬 Australia: Technical Pragmatism
Technology-assisted decision-making (spectral analysis, predictive models), flexible inter-regional blending (South Australia + Barossa), pursuit of consistent quality and batch uniformity, with a cost-effectiveness orientation.
Technology-driven · Flexible blending · Consistent quality · Cross-regional
Dimension 🏛️ Bordeaux 🌟 Napa Valley 🔬 Australia

slides.30.title: The Evolution of Blending Philosophy
slides.30.content:
🏛️ Old World Modernisation
Traditional regions such as Bordeaux are absorbing the technological innovations of the New World while preserving their own terroir identity. The adoption of modern equipment has not altered the fundamental blending philosophy — rather, it enables traditional principles to be executed with greater precision.
Technical modernisation + traditional philosophy = an evolved classic style
🌟 New World Refinement
New World regions are placing increasing emphasis on terroir expression and blending finesse. From their early fruit-forward styles, they have gradually developed blending philosophies with greater complexity and aging potential.
Evolving from simple fruit to complex, elegant style
🌐 The Influence of Globalisation
Demand from international markets and the preferences of leading wine critics are shaping global blending trends — fostering mutual learning and cross-regional exchange, and giving rise to a new standard of "globalised fine wine".
Globalisation drives the exchange and fusion of blending philosophies

slides.33.title: Professional Blending Tasting Techniques
slides.33.content:
👁️ Visual Assessment
Tilt the glass 45° against a white background. Observe colour depth (CS deep purple vs Merlot ruby), tonal harmony, clarity, and brilliance (a pale water rim signals aging potential), then predict the direction of future colour development.
Assess 30–60 sec · Key: tonal harmony · depth consistency
👃 Aroma Analysis
Three-stage approach: top notes (gently smell — CS blackcurrant / Merlot plum / CF violet) → middle notes (swirl, then note oak vanilla / smoke) → finish (assess the empty glass for persistence). In a fine blend, aromas integrate harmoniously.
Assess 2–3 min · Key: layered complexity · harmonious integration
👅 Palate Assessment
Three-stage tasting: entry — burst of fruit; mid-palate — balance of acidity, tannins, and alcohol; finish — length (>60 seconds in outstanding blends). A perfect blend feels seamlessly unified; you sense the whole, not the individual varieties.
Assess 1–2 min · Key: balance · integration · length

slides.34.title: Three Key Exercises for Blending Tasting
slides.34.content:
🎓 Beginner: Variety Identification
First taste each variety individually to learn its character: CS (blackcurrant / high tannins), Merlot (plum / supple), CF (violet / high acidity). Then try simple blends and identify the contribution of each variety.
Success target: correct identification rate > 80%
📊 Intermediate: Ratio Judgement
Learn three fundamental blend types: CS-dominant (>65%, pronounced structure), Merlot-dominant (>60%, fruit-forward), and balanced (CS 50–60%). Complete blind-tasting exercises to estimate the proportion of each variety.
Success target: ratio estimation error < 15%
💡 Advanced: Improvement Suggestions
Scenario exercises: tannins too firm (CS 80%) → suggest raising Merlot to 25–30%; insufficient fruit (CF 20%+) → suggest raising Merlot to 20–30%. Propose 3 or more workable solutions for each case.
Success target: propose 3+ solutions with clear reasoning

slides.35.title: Course Summary and Advanced Learning
slides.35.subtitle: Continued Exploration of the Art of Blending
slides.36.title: Core Key Points Summary of the Art of Blending
slides.36.content:
🎯 Fundamental Principles
Blending creates complexity beyond any single variety's reach (1+1+1>3). CS provides the skeleton; Merlot the flesh; CF adds elegance. Ratios are not merely technical decisions — they reflect the winemaker's aesthetic philosophy. Every 1% adjustment can shift the style.
Blending = Art + Science + Philosophy
🔬 Practical Techniques
Follow a systematic tasting protocol (4–6 min per sample) — never rush to conclusions. Small-sample trials (100–200 ml) are cost-efficient and quickly verifiable. A panel of 5–10 tasters ensures objectivity. Fifty to 100 mini-tastings build the foundation for a final blending decision.
Tasting + Experimentation + Collaboration = Successful blend
🌡️ Decision Factors
Warm vintages: ↑ CF for freshness; cool vintages: ↑ Merlot for roundness (flexible ±10–15% adjustment). Consumer preference is driving a move toward earlier accessibility. Modern tools — spectral analysis, AI assistance, micro-oxygenation — make decisions more precise.
Climate + Market + Technology = Dynamic blending
🚀 Emerging Trends
Old World and New World are learning from each other — the Old World modernising, the New World refining — and the boundaries are blurring. Sustainability concerns are influencing variety selection. The market is shifting from standardised to personalised and differentiated styles, giving winemakers greater freedom to express individuality.
Convergence + Sustainability + Identity = New-era blending
slides.37.title: Advanced Learning Pathways and Recommendations
slides.37.content:
🏭 Practical Advancement
Visit estates to observe the blending process (3–6 months); enrol in WSET/CMS workshops; purchase single-variety wines and conduct your own blending experiments; systematically build a tasting-notes database.
Timeline: 6–12 months · Investment: €2K–10K
📚 Academic Deepening
Study wine chemistry (phenolics / anthocyanins / aromatic molecules); compare global blending philosophies; follow the latest technological developments; conduct in-depth analysis of landmark cases such as Opus One and Sassicaia.
Timeline: 1–2 years · Target: MW / DipWSET qualification
💼 Commercial Application
Research market preference differences (Asia: soft and approachable / Europe–America: structured); learn to balance cost control with quality; master blending story-driven marketing; analyse the younger generation's growing demand for early-drinking wines.
Applications: estate · trade · scoring · education
